n: The Antioch church had a diverse group of leaders: Barnabas from Cyprus, Simeon “the Black,” Lucius from North Africa, Manaen who grew up in Herod Antipas’s court, and Saul from Tarsus.

f.g: Latin for “black” — perhaps describing Simeon’s dark complexion; possibly African.
Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who beheaded John the Baptist.

n: While these leaders worshipped and fasted, the Holy Ghost called Barnabas and Saul to a special mission. The call came by revelation, not by personal ambition.

f.g: Served, worshipped.

n: After more fasting and prayer, the leaders laid their hands on them and sent them out. This setting apart by the laying on of hands is still how callings are given in the Church.
So begins Paul’s first missionary journey (about AD 47–48). They went down to the port of Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus, Barnabas’s home island.

f.g: The seaport serving Antioch, about 16 miles west.

n: At Salamis, on Cyprus’s east coast, they began by teaching in the Jewish synagogues — Paul’s usual pattern. John Mark came along as their assistant.

f.g: Here, an assistant or helper.

n: Crossing the island to Paphos, the Roman capital on the west coast, they met a Jewish magician and false prophet named Bar-jesus.

f.g: Aramaic “son of Joshua/Jesus” — an ironic name for an enemy of Christ.
Greek magos — a magician or occult practitioner.

n: Bar-jesus served as an adviser to the Roman governor, Sergius Paulus. The governor was thoughtful and intelligent, and he sent for the missionaries to hear their message.

f.g: Proconsul — Roman governor of a senatorial province.
Intelligent, wise, discerning.

n: The magician, also called Elymas, worked against the missionaries and tried to keep the governor from believing. He likely feared losing his influence.
From here on Luke uses Paul, Saul’s Roman name, which fits his mission among Gentiles. Filled with the Spirit, Paul fixed his eyes on Elymas.

f.g: Latin Paulus, meaning “small.” Paul likely had both names from birth, as a Jew and a Roman citizen.

n: Paul sharply rebuked Elymas as a deceiver and enemy of righteousness, twisting the Lord’s straight paths. The strong words expose spiritual opposition for what it is.

f.g: Deceit, craftiness.

f.w: pervert the right ways of the Lord

n: Elymas was struck with temporary blindness — the man who blinded others spiritually now groped for someone to lead him. Paul himself once had been led by the hand when blinded.

f.g: For a time — the blindness was temporary, leaving room for repentance.

f.w: seeking some to lead him by the hand

n: The governor believed, amazed not just by the miracle but by the teaching about the Lord. He became one of the first high-ranking Roman converts.

f.w: astonished at the doctrine of the Lord

n: Paul now leads the group. They sailed to Perga on the south coast of modern Turkey, where John Mark left and went home — a decision that later caused a rift between Paul and Barnabas.

f.g: A coastal region of southern Asia Minor (modern Turkey).

n: They traveled inland to another Antioch, in the region of Pisidia. On the Sabbath they went to the synagogue and sat with the congregation.

f.g: A Roman colony in central Asia Minor — different from Antioch in Syria.

n: After readings from the law and the prophets, synagogue leaders often invited visiting teachers to speak. Paul took the opening.

f.g: The scripture readings of a synagogue service: the five books of Moses and a passage from the prophets.
Officials who arranged the service.

n: Paul addressed two groups: Jews (“men of Israel”) and God-fearing Gentiles who worshipped with them. This is Paul’s first recorded sermon.

f.g: Gentiles who believed in Israel’s God and attended synagogue without fully converting.

n: Paul begins with Israel’s story: God chose their ancestors, made them a great people in Egypt, and led them out with power.

f.g: A Hebrew image of mighty, visible power.

f.w: brought he them out of it

n: For forty years God patiently put up with Israel’s behavior in the wilderness. Some ancient manuscripts read “cared for them” instead of “suffered their manners.”

f.g: Bore with their ways; some manuscripts read “carried them as a nurse.”

n: God drove out the seven nations of Canaan and gave Israel the land as an inheritance, divided among the tribes by lot.

f.g: Canaan, in Greek spelling.

n: Then came the era of the judges until Samuel. The 450 years likely counts the whole period from Egypt to the conquest, as many scholars read the Greek.
Israel asked for a king, and God gave them Saul of the tribe of Benjamin — the same tribe as Paul, whose Hebrew name was also Saul.

f.g: Kish, Saul’s father, in Greek spelling.

n: God replaced Saul with David, whom he described as “a man after mine own heart” — someone devoted to doing God’s will.

f.w: a man after mine own heart

n: Here is Paul’s main point: God kept his promise by raising up a Savior, Jesus, from David’s family line.
Before Jesus began his ministry, John the Baptist called all Israel to repent and be baptized, preparing them for the Messiah.
As John’s mission neared its end, he made clear he was not the Messiah. Someone greater was coming, so great that John felt unworthy even to untie his sandals.

f.w: whose shoes of his feet I am not worthy to loose

n: Paul speaks directly to his hearers: this message of salvation is meant for you — both Abraham’s descendants and Gentiles who worship God.

f.w: children of the stock of Abraham

n: The people of Jerusalem and their leaders didn’t recognize Jesus or understand the prophets they read every week — yet in condemning him they fulfilled those very prophecies.

f.w: they have fulfilled them in condemning him

n: Even though they could find no crime deserving death, they pressed Pilate to have Jesus executed.

f.w: they found no cause of death in him

n: Everything prophesied about him came true. They took his body down from the cross — “the tree” — and buried it in a tomb.

f.g: The cross; an allusion to Deuteronomy 21:22-23.

n: Four short words carry the whole gospel: “But God raised him.” Death was not the end of Jesus’ story.

f.w: God raised him from the dead

n: The risen Lord appeared over many days to the disciples who had followed him from Galilee. They are living witnesses of his resurrection.
Paul and Barnabas bring good news: the promise God made to the ancestors of Israel has come true.

f.g: Good news — the meaning of “gospel.”

n: God fulfilled that promise by raising Jesus. Paul quotes Psalm 2, a royal psalm applied to the Messiah as God’s Son.

f.w: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee

n: Jesus rose never to die or decay again. Paul cites Isaiah’s promise of the “sure mercies of David” — the lasting blessings God promised through David’s line.

f.w: I will give you the sure mercies of David

f.g: Decay of the body after death.

n: Paul quotes Psalm 16, just as Peter did at Pentecost: God would not let his Holy One’s body decay.

f.w: Thou shalt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption

n: David served his generation faithfully, then died and was buried, and his body decayed. So the psalm could not have been about David himself.

f.g: Died — a gentle biblical expression for death.

n: But Jesus, whom God raised, did not decay. The prophecy points to him.
Paul brings the sermon to its point: through Jesus, forgiveness of sins is offered to you.
Through Christ, believers are “justified” — declared right with God — in ways the law of Moses alone could never accomplish. This is a central theme Paul later develops in Romans.

f.g: Declared righteous, forgiven and accepted by God.

f.w: could not be justified by the law of Moses

n: Paul ends with a warning: don’t let the prophets’ warnings come true for you.
He quotes Habakkuk: God would do something so astonishing that scoffers would refuse to believe it even when told. Paul applies it to the work of Christ.

f.w: Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish
I work a work in your days

n: As the people left, the Gentiles in particular begged to hear more the following Sabbath.
Many Jews and converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who encouraged them to keep relying on God’s grace.

f.g: Gentiles who had fully converted to Judaism.

f.w: continue in the grace of God

n: Word spread fast. The next Sabbath, nearly the whole city gathered to hear the message.
Some Jewish leaders, jealous of the crowds, began contradicting Paul and speaking abusively. Envy, not doctrine, drove the opposition.

f.g: Here, speaking insults and abuse.

n: Paul and Barnabas boldly explained: we had to preach to you first, but since you reject it, we will turn to the Gentiles. The gospel went first to the Jews, then to all.

f.w: first have been spoken to you

n: They cited Isaiah’s prophecy of the Lord’s servant being a light to the Gentiles. The mission to all nations was part of God’s plan all along.
The Gentiles rejoiced, and those prepared for eternal life believed. Latter-day Saints may see in “ordained” a hint of premortal preparation, though the Greek can also mean “disposed” or “appointed.”

f.g: Greek tetagmenoi — appointed, set in order, disposed.

n: The gospel message spread throughout the surrounding region.

f.g: Spread abroad, made known.

n: Opponents turned influential women and city leaders against the missionaries and had them driven out of the area.

f.g: Borders, territory.

n: Paul and Barnabas shook the dust from their feet, a sign Jesus had taught, showing they were free of responsibility. Then they moved on to Iconium.

f.w: shook off the dust of their feet

f.g: Modern Konya, Turkey, about 90 miles southeast.

n: Despite persecution, the new disciples were full of joy and the Holy Ghost. True joy does not depend on easy circumstances.
